title: The one who lit a fire
hookLine: the hypocrites are like a man who lights a fire, then the light is taken (2:17)

cards: Night, in open country, no moon. A man gathers sticks, strikes a flame, and blows on it until it catches. For a minute the circle around him lights up: the rocks, the path, the faces of whoever's with him.

Then, all at once, the light is gone, and the dark is darker than before, because his eyes had already adjusted to the fire. That's the picture al-Baqarah paints in verse seventeen. Today: the one who lit a fire.

teach.b: The opening of al-Baqarah describes three kinds of people. The mindful, whom you met yesterday. Those who refuse outright.
And, at the greatest length, a third group: those who say we believe, but whose hearts don't follow.

The commentators identify them as the munafiqun, the hypocrites, a name the Qur'an uses in other surahs; in Medina it meant people who joined the community outwardly while working against it. Then the parable.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO KINDLED A FIRE
teach.b: In Pickthall's words: “Their likeness is as the likeness of one who kindleth fire.” The fire lights up everything around him, and then God takes away their light and leaves them in darkness where they cannot see.
Notice what the parable doesn't say. It doesn't say they never had light. They lit the fire themselves.
They saw. The tragedy is light that was had and then lost. A second picture follows straight after: a storm at night, rain, thunder, lightning.
When the lightning flashes, they walk a few steps by it. When it goes dark, they stand still. Faith by flashes.
Now the turn. Early Muslims didn't treat warnings like this only as a description of other people.
Bukhari records a saying of the follower Ibn Abi Mulaykah: he met thirty of the companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and every one of them feared hypocrisy for himself.
The people closest to the Prophet read such warnings as a mirror. Not are they hypocrites, but am I letting my own light go out?

how: Muslim teachers often read the Qur'an's verses about hypocrisy as a warning to oneself rather than a label for others, and many traditional supplications ask God to keep the heart firm.

o: newcomers still learning how to pray right
those who openly refuse to believe at all
hypocrites, who say we believe but don't mean it

games.q: the first parables — tap the pairs.
p: light that was had, then taken
a few steps, then standing still
saying we believe, hearts not following

s: in the parable, the man never had any light
he lit the fire himself; the light was had, and then taken.
the companions feared hypocrisy in themselves, not only in others
Ibn Abi Mulaykah said thirty of them each feared it for himself.

games.q: you've just heard a warning about hypocrisy. what did the companions, as Bukhari reports, do with warnings like it?
o: make a list of who it meant.
games.why: they feared it for themselves. the verse became a mirror, not a finger.

practice: Think of one good thing you once had and let slip: a habit of prayer, a morning walk, calling your grandmother, reading a little each night. Not to feel guilty, just to see it, like a fire you once lit.
Hold it gently as you breathe, and choose one small way you might tend it again.

wordCard.voice: Munafiqun. The hypocrites: those in al-Baqarah's parable who lit a fire, saw by it, and then lost the light.

orig.note: Arabic: hypocrisy; the hypocrites are al-munafiqun.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the light lit. The warning is a mirror, not a finger. Until tomorrow.
